Se souvenir et agir, disent les aînés: Remember and act, say the elders
Le territoire des Syilx forme un magnifi: Syilx territory is a magnificent and richly varied landscape of deserts, lakes, alpine forests and grasslands.
Suikiʔst Pauline Terbasket, de la Nation: Suikiʔst Pauline Terbasket, of the Sylix Nation
La semaine dernière avait lieu la toute: Last week saw the very first National Day for Truth and Reconciliation, followed by the International Day of Older Persons on October 1. September 30 is meant to shine more light and attention on Indigenous peoples, on residential school survivors and on those who never came home. For the International Day of Older Persons, three Indigenous elders shared their reflections, their feelings and the calls to action they say are needed. Suikiʔst Pauline Terbasket is a proud member of the Syilx Nation. Syilx territory is a magnificent and richly varied landscape of deserts, lakes, alpine forests and grasslands. This transboundary territory stretches from Washington State to the Okanagan region of British Columbia.
Terbasket s'est réveillée le 30 septembr: Terbasket woke up on September 30 feeling as though she were getting up to prepare for a memorial or a funeral. Alongside that feeling was “knowing that many people are determined to take action across Turtle Island,” she says. She went over all her plans for the day. Although her office at the Okanagan Nation Alliance was closed for the day, she imagines that for many people, it was a day like any other. Scrolling through her Facebook news feed, as she does every morning, she saw a flood of “orange” messages paying tribute to survivors of Indigenous residential schools. The stream of posts carried the same message: “I am here because my parents/grandparents survived Indian residential schools.” One post caught her attention. “It said: ‘I am here because my ancestors were beautiful.’ My tears flowed,” says Suikiʔst Pauline Terbasket. The strength of that message captures the full scale of the situation.
« À travers le brouillard de la déposses: “Through the fog of dispossession, stolen children, violence, poverty, the internalized distress of self, of others and of the world. And yet, they are so beautiful, courageous and determined — for their own health, for the love of their families, their homes, their lands, their peoples.”
Suikiʔst Pauline Terbasket réfléchit ens: Suikiʔst Pauline Terbasket then thought about what her own “I am here” message would be.
« Je suis ici parce que j'ai été aimée,: “I am here because I have been loved, and I am grateful to be able to advocate for social justice, for change, and for how brilliant we all are,” she says.
Terbasket ne considère pas seulement sa: Terbasket thinks not only of her own nation but of Indigenous peoples on Turtle Island and around the world. “To be given another day of life today, so that I can remember and never forget what Indigenous peoples have endured for generations, and for the generations to come.”
Le maintien du feu sacré, pour les tombe: Keeping the sacred fire burning for the graves of the children who were found. Photo: Suikiʔst Pauline Terbasket.
Terbasket dit que le 30 septembre est «: Terbasket says September 30 is “so we don't forget that much more has to be done. The act was, and still is, genocide. There will be no more genocide.” She reflects on the fact that the federal government established a National Day for Truth and Reconciliation. “Whose truth? Who needs reconciliation?” asks Terbasket. “Days designated as ‘official’ fall far short of ever achieving a just society for Indigenous peoples, settlers and colonial governments, because it is an external measure.” Terbasket points to the many levels of personal work needed for transformation, whether at work, in personal life and/or in everyday activities. To calm the mind, she suggests that people replenish themselves through the land and take part in ceremonies.
L'aînée crie et métisse Mabel Nipshank h: Cree and Métis elder Mabel Nipshank dressed for the occasion. Photo: Shushan Vardanyan.
Mabel Nipshank, aînée crie et métisse, e: Mabel Nipshank, a Cree and Métis elder, is a dedicated longtime activist, known for her housing advocacy work with the <l1>Downtown Eastside Women's Centre in Vancouver</l1>. She examines the impact of colonialism's destruction of the matriarchal system, more specifically, the normalization of violence against women. In her work titled “Aboriginal women: no rights to land or children,” she describes the additional obstacles placed in the way of women seeking custody of their children and visiting rights. Holding back a flood of emotions, Cree/Métis elder Mabel Nipshank speaks of the contrast with the scale of the phenomenon.
« La destruction à grande échelle, contr: “Large-scale destruction, set against a date officially declared the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation, is a disgrace, another slap in the face,” she says. Her thoughts go to “Indigenous communities that have been so badly affected — beyond all repair.”
« Nous sommes toujours là ». Kukdookaa T: “We are still here.” Kukdookaa Terri Brown and her sister Lila Corcoran of the Tahltan Nation. Photo courtesy of Kukdookaa Terri Brown.
Le territoire de la Nation Tahl-tan couv: The territory of the Tahltan Nation covers a vast area of northwestern British Columbia, 95,933 square kilometres. That is the equivalent of 11% of the province, and it includes the Stikine watershed. Kukdookaa Terri Brown is a member of the Crow clan of the Tahltan Nation.
Elle a occupé le poste de cheffe de son: She has served as chief of her people and was also president of the Native Women's Association of Canada. During her six years with the Truth and Reconciliation Commission of Canada, she heard many stories of children who went missing or who never returned from residential schools. She is also a residential school survivor. “The National Day for Truth and Reconciliation means that we are recognized in this country for the human rights violations and the genocide,” says Kukdookaa.
À ce titre, elle affirme que cette journ: As such, she says this day must be an occasion to remember “those who couldn't come home and those who survived.” Kukdookaa calls for action, drawing on her voice as a respected elder. “We need to move from remembrance to action.
Mettez fin au racisme, au sexisme, à la: End racism, sexism, poverty and injustice in all their forms. We are still here,” she says. “We must be relentless in everything we do to move toward a more just society and to contribute to it.”
